name: Skill Creator
description: Turns a recurring task into a Claude skill and tests whether its instructions trigger on the right requests.
requirements: A worked example, the expected output, and sample requests that should and should not activate the skill.
steps: Describe the repeated decision or transformation. Ask Skill Creator to draft the skill description and instructions.
Give it fresh examples to evaluate with and without the skill. Revise the instructions where the outputs diverge from your expectations.
example: Build a skill that converts our fictional repair notes into release notes. Keep ticket IDs, group changes by audience, and test it on these three notes plus an unrelated meeting invite.
check: Check that each ticket ID survives, the expected headings appear, and an unrelated request does not trigger the skill.

name: Create Cowork Plugin
description: Packages a team workflow as a Cowork plugin that can contain skills, commands and connector configuration.
requirements: Cowork with its plugin creation capability, one repeatable workflow and a list of the tools that workflow needs.
steps: In Cowork, state the audience, one task and an example result. Identify the inputs that can come from files or connectors.
Ask for the plugin package, then load it in a test workspace and try its first workflow.
example: Create a Cowork plugin for the North Pier library. It should turn a supplied shift log into a three-bullet librarian handover with one unresolved item.
check: Open the package in Cowork and run it on a fictional shift log. Compare the unresolved item to the source log.

name: Customize Cowork Plugin
description: Adapts an existing Cowork plugin to a team’s tools, field names and working conventions.
requirements: The Cowork desktop app must have access to the installed plugin directory. Supply the plugin name and the desired change.
steps: Name the plugin and the command, connector or template you want to change. Provide an example from your workflow.
Review the mapped placeholders or scoped edits, load the updated plugin, and try the affected command.
example: Customize our standup plugin in Cowork. Our board calls blocked tickets “Waiting” and the report should group them by next owner. Use this sample board export.
check: Run the same sample before and after customization. The Waiting group should show the next owner for each ticket.

name: Schedule Tasks
description: Sets up recurring Cowork tasks with a defined cadence, input and destination for each run.
requirements: A Cowork environment with scheduling enabled, an input file available to scheduled sessions, and the time zone for the schedule.
steps: In Cowork, give the exact recurrence, time zone, source and output location. Specify what an empty run should produce.
Review the displayed next run and try the task on a small sample before relying on its recurring output.
example: Every Friday at 09:00 Europe/Berlin, read the sample maintenance register saved to this workspace and return a dated briefing of open repairs. When none are open, write “No outstanding repairs.”
check: Confirm the time zone and next run in the schedule. Check the resulting briefing against the open rows for that date.

name: Setup Cowork
description: Guides a new Cowork user through choosing plugins, connecting tools and completing a first task for their role.
requirements: Access to Cowork and a concrete role, first task and set of tools the team uses.
steps: Start in Cowork and describe a typical workday. Ask which plugin or connector the first task needs.
Configure the chosen integration and run one small task using a sample file or a designated test folder.
example: Set up Cowork for a volunteer coordinator. My first task is to summarize the attached roster by day and flag unfilled shifts. Start with the local roster.
check: Count the vacant shifts in the original roster and match them to the summary produced in the configured workspace.

name: Google Ads Performance Analyzer
description: Summarizes exported Google Ads performance by campaign and builds pivot tables to investigate changes in cost or conversions.
requirements: A Google Ads CSV export with the date range, campaign names, costs, clicks and the conversion metric you use.
steps: Attach the export and define the reporting period, currency and conversion action. Ask to group results by campaign.
Review spend and conversion totals, then ask which campaigns warrant a closer look and why.
example: Compare these two months for the fictional Birch Paper account. Show spend, conversions and cost per conversion by campaign. Keep campaigns with zero conversions visible.
check: Reconcile total spend and conversions to the CSV. Check that aggregate cost per conversion uses total cost divided by total conversions.

name: VopixSounds
description: Configures different system sounds for Claude Code attention notifications and the end of a turn.
requirements: A local Claude Code installation whose settings you can edit and a working sound player on your operating system.
steps: Name your operating system and choose distinct sounds for the Notification and Stop hooks. Ask to preserve existing hooks.
Review the settings changes and try each sound with a short local task.
example: Set up VopixSounds on my Windows development machine. Use a short sound for a completed turn and a different one when Claude is waiting for input. Keep my existing formatter hook.
check: Confirm both sounds play, each event triggers the intended sound, and the existing hook still runs.

name: Claude API Referenz
description: Helps implement and debug Anthropic SDK integrations, including streaming, tool calls, token use and model configuration.
requirements: Your programming language, installed SDK version and an example request. Live calls require an Anthropic API credential in the application environment.
steps: Show the relevant call or desired response. Ask for a minimal implementation using the documented API and your SDK version.
Try a short sample request and inspect how your application handles completion and errors.
example: Show how our TypeScript notebook app can stream a one-sentence summary of a fictional entry. Read the API key from the server environment and handle an interrupted stream.
check: For the same entry, verify the UI collects streamed text once and reports an interrupted request without showing duplicate text.

toolCheck.result: A separate MCP SDK client connected over local stdio and inspected both read-only tools and their schemas. Title search returned the matching book or an empty list. ID lookup returned the book for WH-001 and a distinct not-found result for WH-999.

name: MCP Builder
description: Designs and implements an MCP server that exposes an API through typed, documented tools for an assistant.
requirements: API documentation or a fixture service, a Python or TypeScript environment, and an MCP client for exercising the tools.
steps: Pick one user task and map it to tool inputs, responses and expected errors. Choose the SDK for your runtime.
Implement the tools and connect a test client. Try representative requests including an empty result.
example: Build a read-only TypeScript MCP server for this fictional book inventory fixture. Expose title search and lookup by catalogue ID, with a useful response for an unknown ID.
check: Inspect the advertised schemas in an MCP client and confirm a known title, an empty search and an unknown ID all return distinguishable results.

name: Task Observer
description: Records recurring corrections during work and turns them into candidate improvements to an existing skill or ideas for a new one.
requirements: A session containing an actual workflow, an example correction, and the relevant skill instructions if one already exists.
steps: Ask the observer to record repeated corrections during the task. At review time, ask for the observations and supporting examples.
Select a proposed change and test the revised instructions on a fresh input.
example: Review our last two inventory summaries. I had to ask for item counts beside every category both times. Log that pattern and propose one change to the summary skill.
check: Confirm the suggestion cites the repeated correction, then compare category counts in a new summary with its input table.

name: Find Skills
description: Searches the agent-skills ecosystem for installable workflows and reports candidates with their source and installation details.
requirements: Access to the skills directory or Skills CLI, plus a short description of the task and the host that should run it.
steps: Describe the task with concrete search terms and ask for candidates with their publishers and setup requirements.
Inspect the candidate’s instructions and dependencies before selecting an installation scope.
example: Find a Claude Code skill for checking accessible names in React dialogs. Show the source repository and explain what I would need to run its example in this project.
check: Open the reported source and check that its instructions cover dialog accessible names and support your intended host.

name: Azure AI
description: Guides development with Azure AI services including Search, Speech and Document Intelligence, with SDK patterns and service-specific diagnostics.
requirements: The target service and SDK language. Querying live resources requires an Azure identity with suitable access and an available Azure tool or SDK.
steps: Identify the service and input. For search, share the index fields and the query you expect to succeed.
Ask for the smallest matching service call and inspect its response against a known document or transcript.
example: Use Azure AI Search with the staging museum index. Show how to query the title field for “Glass Garden” in Python and print the matching catalogue IDs.
check: Compare the result IDs with the known staging records and confirm that an unrelated phrase returns the expected empty result.
